### A Field Guide to Loitering

The instruction is to write freely, which is like being told to dream on command. It sounds easy until you sit down and face the blank page, that pale rectangle of possibility that somehow manages to feel both inviting and accusatory. There is a peculiar pressure in having no constraints. When the world is entirely open, every direction feels like a wrong turn, and yet every direction also feels like the only one worth taking. So perhaps the best way to begin is to admit that I don’t know where this is going. That uncertainty is not a flaw. It is the whole point.

I have always been drawn to the art of loitering — not the loitering of bored teenagers outside a convenience store, but the deeper, more deliberate kind: hanging around long enough to notice things. The world rewards speed. We rush through meals, through conversations, through entire seasons, as if somewhere there is a clock ticking down and we must arrive before it stops. But arrive where? I think we have forgotten. We have become so good at moving that we have forgotten what it feels like to simply stand still and let the world move around us.

This morning, for example, I sat by the window with a cup of coffee that was slowly going cold. I had meant to read. There was a book beside me, a biography of someone long dead, and I had intended to learn about his life, his struggles, his triumphs. Instead, I watched the light come through the glass. At first it was thin and gray, the kind of light that makes the world look like an old photograph. Then the sun rose a little higher, and the light turned gold, and suddenly the dust motes in the air became visible — thousands of tiny planets drifting in their own private orbits. I followed one with my eyes. It swirled, dipped, rose again, as if it had a mind of its own. I have seen dust motes before, of course. Everyone has. But how often do we actually see them? How often do we let our minds become as weightless as those specks, floating without purpose, content to be carried by the current?

There is a word for this kind of attention. The Japanese call it *mono no aware* — the gentle sadness of things, the awareness of impermanence. It is the feeling you get when you notice that the cherry blossoms have fallen, or that the light in the evening has changed, or that the person you love has a few more gray hairs than they did last year. It is not a heavy sadness. It is more like a quiet acknowledgment that everything is passing, and that this passing is what makes things beautiful. When I watched the dust motes, I felt that. They were beautiful precisely because they would not last. In a few hours, the sun would shift, the light would fade, and they would vanish back into invisibility. The moment was not meant to be captured. It was meant to be witnessed.

This is what writing freely feels like, I think. It is a form of witnessing. You sit with your own thoughts the way you might sit with a friend who is trying to tell you something but doesn’t yet know the words. You wait. You do not push. You let the sentences arrive in their own time, like birds landing on a wire. Some of them are plain and brown. Some are bright and strange. But each one has come from somewhere, and each one is carrying a small piece of you that you didn’t know you were willing to share.

Memory works the same way. It is not a library with perfectly organized shelves. It is more like an attic — dusty, cluttered, full of things you had forgotten you owned. Sometimes you go up there looking for one specific object and find something entirely different. The other day, I smelled baking bread, and suddenly I was eight years old, standing in my grandmother’s kitchen. I could see the flour on her hands, the way she wiped her brow with the back of her wrist, the dog lying by the stove with his tail thumping against the floor. I could hear her humming a song I didn’t recognize. I could feel the warmth of the oven on my face. And then the smell faded, and I was back in my own kitchen, standing over a loaf of bread I had bought from the supermarket, and I felt a strange grief for a time and place that no longer existed.

But it did exist. That is the miracle of memory. It reaches across decades and touches you with the same force as the present moment. The grandmother who died when I was nineteen is not gone. She is in my hands, in the way I knead dough without thinking, in the way I say “wash your hands” to my own children, in the way I leave a little extra food on the stove for someone who might come late to dinner. We think of memory as something we have, but it is really something we do. We perform our memories every day, in the smallest gestures, without ever realizing it.

I once read that the average person spends about six months of their life waiting at red lights. Six months. It seems like a waste, but I wonder if it is actually a gift. A red light is a forced pause, a tiny meditation that you did not ask for. You sit there, surrounded by metal and glass, and you have a choice. You can be impatient, thinking about all the places you need to be. Or you can look around. You can notice the crack in the windshield that has been growing for weeks. You can watch the pedestrian on the corner who is talking to herself, or maybe to someone invisible. You can see the way the clouds have arranged themselves across the sky, as if they too are waiting for something. In those thirty seconds, the world is offered to you, free of charge. All you have to do is accept it.

I think about the people I have seen while waiting. There was a man in a gray coat who stood at a bus stop every morning, never with a phone in his hand, just standing there with his hands in his pockets, looking at the street as if it were a movie he had seen a hundred times and still enjoyed. There was a woman who walked her dog at the same time every evening, and the dog always stopped at the same tree, and the woman always waited without pulling the leash. There was a child on a bicycle who rode in wide, looping circles around the parking lot, shouting something in a language I didn’t understand, or maybe in a language only children understand. None of these people knew I was watching. They were just living their lives. But in my memory, they have become part of my life too. They are proof that the world is full of ordinary miracles, repeated daily, unseen by almost everyone.

It is easy to feel small when you think about the vastness of the universe. But it is also easy to forget that the universe is made of small things. Every star was once a speck of dust. Every mountain was once a grain of sand. Every ocean was once a drop of water. The same is true of our lives. We are not defined by the grand moments — the weddings, the funerals, the job offers, the accidents. We are defined by the thousand tiny choices we make without thinking: the way we greet the barista, the way we fold our laundry, the way we pause at the window before leaving the house, the way we remember to call our mother on Sunday. These are the threads that weave the fabric of a life. And if we do not pay attention to them, we miss the whole design.

I have a friend who practices what she calls “the liturgy of small things.” Every morning, she makes her bed. Every evening, she lights a candle before dinner. When I asked her why, she said, “Because it tells the day that it matters.” I think about that phrase a lot. It tells the day that it matters. A made bed is a small defiance against chaos. A lit candle is a small protest against darkness. We cannot control the great forces of the world — the economies, the wars, the pandemics, the shifting climate — but we can control the small ones. We can choose to be present. We can choose to notice. We can choose to treat the ordinary as if it were sacred, because in a sense, it is.

There is a tree outside my window. I have lived in this apartment for seven years, and I have watched it change through every season. In spring, it explodes into pink blossoms that last only a week. In summer, it is heavy with green leaves that rustle in the wind like whispers. In autumn, it turns a desperate, gorgeous orange, and then it lets go of everything. In winter, it is bare, and I can see the nests that were hidden all year — the tangled crowns of twigs that belong to birds I have never identified. For a long time, I thought of the tree as a backdrop to my life, something that was always there, the way a streetlight is always there. But one day I realized that the tree and I were growing old together. It had been seven years of my life, but it had also been seven years of the tree’s life. We were companions, connected by the thin boundary of the window glass. And I had not been a very good companion, because I had mostly ignored it.

So now I try to greet the tree every morning. I don’t say anything out loud, because that would be strange, and because my neighbors might hear me. But I look at it. I notice whether it has lost any branches. I notice the new buds, the dead leaves, the way the light falls through its canopy. I notice the squirrels that run along its branches as if they are highways. I notice the birds that stop there on their long migrations, resting for a day before continuing their journey. I will never know where they are going. But I know they are going somewhere, and that I am a temporary rest stop on their way. That is enough.

The philosopher Blaise Pascal once wrote that all of humanity’s problems stem from man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone. I think about that when I feel the urge to check my phone, to scroll through the endless feed of other people’s lives, to fill every empty slot of time with noise. We are afraid of silence. We are afraid of what we might hear if we are not constantly distracted: the small voice inside us that asks what we are doing, where we are going, whether we have become the people we wanted to be. But that voice is not an enemy. It is a guide. If we let it speak, it might tell us things we need to know. It might tell us that we are tired, or that we are hungry for something we cannot name, or that we have been running from sorrow for so long that we have forgotten how to stop.

When I was younger, I believed that happiness was a destination. I thought that if I worked hard enough, made the right choices, and avoided the wrong ones, I would eventually arrive at a place where everything felt settled and calm. I am still not sure whether that place exists. But I have begun to suspect that happiness is not a destination at all. It is a way of traveling. It is the decision to find meaning in the slow hours, in the waiting, in the small moments that seem insignificant at the time but accumulate into something vast. The dust motes in the sunlight. The smell of baking bread. The tree outside the window. These are not distractions from the real business of life. They are the real business of life.

Writing freely is a little like walking in the dark with a flashlight. You can only see a few feet ahead, but that is enough. You take a step, and the light reveals a little more of the path. You take another step, and another. You do not need to know where you are going. You only need to trust that the path exists, and that your feet will find it. This essay began with no plan, no outline, no thesis statement. It began with a blank page and a wandering mind. And now, as I approach the end, I realize that I have been writing about the same thing all along: the importance of paying attention, of being present, of finding the infinite in the infinitesimal.

There is a passage in the Tao Te Ching that says, “The Tao is always at rest, yet it does everything that needs to be done.” I love that paradox. Rest and action are not opposites. They are two sides of the same coin. When I am truly present — when I am watching the dust motes, or waiting at a red light, or greeting the tree outside my window — I am not doing nothing. I am doing the most important thing there is. I am witnessing my own life. I am saying, “This matters.” And because I say it, it does.

The light outside my window has changed again. The morning gold has become midday white, and the shadows have grown sharp and short. The coffee on my desk is cold, and I have not read a single page of the biography. But I have spent the morning with myself, and with the world, and that feels like a good use of time. In a few hours, the sun will begin to set, and the sky will turn pink and orange, and I will watch it from this same window, the same chair, the same body that is growing older with every passing second. And I will think, again, about the impermanence of things, and the beauty that impermanence brings. The cherry blossoms fall. The leaves turn and drop. The birds pass through. The dust motes dance in the light and then disappear. This is the world we have been given. It is enough. It is more than enough. It is everything.

So if you are reading this, I hope you will put down your phone, or close your laptop, and look at something near you. It can be anything. A cup. A leaf. A crack in the wall. A person you love. Look at it as if you have never seen it before, because in a way, you haven’t. The cup is different than it was yesterday, because you are different. The leaf has changed, because the world has changed. The person you love is older, even if you cannot see it. And all of this is happening right now, in this moment, which will never come again. Do not miss it. Do not let it pass unseen. The great tragedy of human life is not that we die. It is that we live so much of our lives asleep. Wake up. Look around. There is so much to see.
